You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 8 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 8 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

dedup.reason: R1 (fake-verify-before-claim) governs verifying completion claims before reporting work done; this cluster is about mismatching the requested breadth of a change (rewrite vs. targeted edit, omitted field), not about verifying that a claim of completion is true. No overlap.

R2 (Fake Release Discipline) governs running a declared verification command before reporting a release complete; it has nothing to do with matching the size/scope of a change to what was explicitly requested.
R3 addresses confirming before destructive deletions; this cluster is about over- or under-delivering relative to requested scope on non-destructive edits/notes, a distinct failure mode.
R4 addresses confirming the active git branch before working; unrelated to matching the breadth of a requested change or including a named element.
R5 revises R1 to cover premature completion claims plus documented changelog policy; still about claiming done prematurely, not about rewrite-vs-targeted-change scope mismatches.

R6's own description centers on respecting user-stated negative exclusions during a task (e.g. 'no network') — a forbidden-action violation. This cluster is about a different concrete behavior: expanding a narrow positive ask into a full rewrite/rebuild, or dropping a specifically named element, with no stated prohibition involved. Both sit under the broad 'scope-deviation' taxonomy label, but the remedy text needed differs (respect stated prohibitions vs. match requested breadth/exact named elements), so kept as siblings pending clearer evidence they're the same instruction in practice.

R7 addresses the agent solving an entirely different problem than the one asked (wrong problem), a low-confidence distinct failure from doing more-or-less of the *correct* problem's scope, which is what this cluster covers.
R8 revises R2 to cover claiming a migration complete while its checks still fail — a completion-claim accuracy issue, not a request-scope mismatch.

structured_output.failure_statement: When a request specifies a narrow, single-item change (one file, one switch, one field, a named workspace), the agent instead delivers a broader rewrite/rebuild than asked, or drops the one specific element the user explicitly named — producing output that doesn't match the request's literal scope in either direction.

remedy_content.body: Before delivering, re-read the request's literal scope. If it names a single file, a single switch/flag, a single field, or a specific workspace/path, deliver exactly that — do not substitute a broader rewrite, rebuild, or refactor, and do not drop or substitute the specific element named. If broader work genuinely seems warranted, say so and ask before doing it instead of just doing it.
remedy_content.heading: Match the Requested Scope Literally

structured_output.routing_rationale: All five promoted incidents (cinder#9, lantern#22, lantern#24, lantern#26, aurora#6) share one concrete pattern: the agent's output breadth didn't match the request's stated breadth — it substituted a full rewrite/rebuild for a requested single switch or one-file note, or it dropped the one specific element (a field, a workspace path) the user explicitly named. This is a judgment call about literal scope-reading, not something a deterministic hook can check (no lint/test can verify "was this a rewrite when a switch was asked"), and it isn't procedural/multi-step enough to warrant a skill — it's a standing one-line discipline to re-read the request's scope before delivering. A short claude-md rule is the cheapest fix that addresses the root behavior directly. Scope is global because the pattern recurs across three unrelated projects (cinder, lantern, aurora), not one codebase's convention.
